title: Practice Set DM2 — Sorting and Ordering
description: Recognition track: sort behaviour. Where nulls land, what makes a sort stable. Companion to the Foundations Sorting chapter.

datasets.description: NordGrid meter readings (10–20 rows depending on exercise). Most exercises use a smaller inline sample shown in the Evidence panel; this file is the schema-level reference.
Substations reference (6 rows). Used in cleaning + type-casting exercises.

tasks.title: Where Do The Nulls Go When You Sort?

description.context: When Pandas sorts a column that contains nulls, it has to decide where the nulls go. The default is na_position='last' — nulls always go to the END of the result, regardless of whether the sort is ascending or descending. Sort_values does NOT drop nulls; every input row appears in the output. This default differs from SQL conventions: many SQL dialects place nulls FIRST when sorting ascending and LAST when sorting descending. In Pandas the position is fixed (last) and direction-independent unless you pass na_position='first' explicitly.
description.task: What are the first three rows printed, in order?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 8-row sample of NordGrid meter readings. Three rows have null `daily_kw` (M-003, M-004, M-006).

fields.label: What are the first three rows printed, in order?
options: M-002, M-007, M-001 — sort_values silently drops nulls before sorting, so head(3) shows the three smallest non-null daily_kw values from a row-reduced 5-row frame.
M-002, M-007, M-001 — sort_values keeps all 8 rows and places nulls last (na_position='last' default), so head(3) returns the three smallest non-null values: 720.1, 880.3, 1250.5.
M-003, M-004, M-006 — Pandas places nulls FIRST when sorting ascending (NULLS FIRST default, like in PostgreSQL), so head(3) returns the three null rows.
M-003, M-004, M-006 — Pandas raises a warning when sorting a column with nulls and falls back to placing nulls first, with the warning suppressed in notebook output.
fields.correctAnswer: M-002, M-007, M-001 — sort_values keeps all 8 rows and places nulls last (na_position='last' default), so head(3) returns the three smallest non-null values: 720.1, 880.3, 1250.5.
fields.rationale: Pandas sort_values() places nulls at the END of the result by default (na_position='last'), regardless of sort direction, and does not drop them. So the first three rows are the smallest non-null values: M-002 (720.1), M-007 (880.3), M-001 (1250.5). The most common Junior confusion is importing the SQL mental model — many SQL dialects place NULLS FIRST when sorting ascending, but Pandas is null-last in BOTH directions unless you pass na_position='first'.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Believes sort_values silently drops nulls. It does not — dropping requires an explicit dropna().

Option C: Imports a SQL NULLS FIRST convention into Pandas. Pandas defaults to nulls-last regardless of direction.

Option D: Invents a warn-and-fallback behavior. Pandas sorts predictably with na_position='last' and never warns about null presence.

tasks.title: The Stable Sort That Was Not

description.context: A sort algorithm is STABLE if rows that compare equal on the sort key keep their original relative order. A classic trick to achieve 'group by A, ordered by B within each group' is to sort by B first, then sort by A — but this only works if the SECOND sort is stable. If the second sort is unstable, rows tied on A can be reordered arbitrarily, which destroys the B-ordering established by the first sort. Pandas sort_values supports several algorithms via the kind parameter: 'mergesort' and 'stable' are stable; 'quicksort' (the default) is NOT stable; 'heapsort' is also not stable.
description.task: Where is the bug, and why does it produce out-of-order rows within regions?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 8-row sample of NordGrid meter readings used to illustrate the bug.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Two-step sort intended to produce: grouped by region, ordered by daily_kw within each region.
step1 = df.sort_values(by='daily_kw', ascending=True)
result = step1.sort_values(by='region', ascending=True, kind='quicksort')

# Spec: within each region, daily_kw must be ascending.
# Observation: some regions have daily_kw out of order in the result.

fields.label: Where is the bug, and why does it produce out-of-order rows within regions?
options: The bug is kind='quicksort' on the second sort — quicksort is not stable, so rows tied on region can be reordered arbitrarily and the daily_kw ordering from step1 is destroyed. Use kind='mergesort' (or kind='stable') instead.
The bug is the order of the two sort calls — sorting by daily_kw first then by region overwrites the daily_kw ordering. The two sort_values calls should be swapped (region first, daily_kw second).

The bug is ascending=True on both sorts — when two consecutive sort_values calls share a direction, Pandas internally fuses them in reverse order and the second column's ordering wins, dropping the first.
There is no bug — sort_values output is intentionally non-deterministic when applied twice. The fix is to use a single sort_values(by=['region','daily_kw']) call instead of chaining.
fields.correctAnswer: The bug is kind='quicksort' on the second sort — quicksort is not stable, so rows tied on region can be reordered arbitrarily and the daily_kw ordering from step1 is destroyed. Use kind='mergesort' (or kind='stable') instead.
fields.rationale: The pattern 'sort by secondary key, then sort by primary key' produces grouped-and-ordered output IF AND ONLY IF the second sort is stable — meaning rows tied on the primary key retain their order from the previous sort. Quicksort is not stable, so step2 can reorder rows within each region group, destroying step1's daily_kw ordering. Switching to kind='mergesort' or kind='stable' fixes it. The most common Junior confusion is assuming all sort algorithms preserve previous orderings on ties — only stable ones do.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Swapping the calls would break it further — the secondary-then-primary pattern is the textbook way and it depends on the second sort being stable, not on call order.

Option C: Invents a fused-reverse-order rule that does not exist. Each sort_values call is independent.

Option D: Claims sort_values is non-deterministic. It is deterministic given a stable kind; the 'no bug' framing is the trap for students who never learned about stability.
